tours.title: One signal, one order
tours.summary: How Venture DAO's trading engine makes sure a retried or duplicated signal can never open a second position, and refuses trades that can't pay for their own fees.

steps.title: Every trade gets a name
steps.note: An intended trade is identified by account, symbol, direction and the minute it happened. A restart, a double-click or two overlapping ticks all produce the same key, so the engine can recognise them as the same trade.

steps.title: Reserve the key before sending
steps.note: The key is reserved before the order goes out, not after it comes back. If the exchange call fails halfway, the order might already be live, so the key stays used and a retry is suppressed instead of becoming a second position.

steps.title: Refuse trades that only pay fees
steps.note: This check exists because of my own result: 31 winning trades and the account still down 6%. The losses were fees and slippage, not direction, so a trade whose target is worth less than three round trips of costs is blocked.

tours.title: Keeping exchange keys safe
tours.summary: Venture DAO stores users' exchange API secrets. This is the code that encrypts them, binds each one to its owner, and keeps them out of logs.

steps.title: Why this cipher
steps.note: GCM authenticates as well as encrypts: a tampered record fails to decrypt instead of quietly returning altered bytes. The IV is random every time and never taken from a caller, because reusing one breaks GCM completely.
steps.code:
* AES-256-GCM rather than CBC: GCM authenticates the ciphertext, so a record
 * that has been tampered with fails to decrypt instead of silently yielding
 * altered bytes. A record's IV is random per encryption and stored alongside
 * it — reusing an IV under the same key is the one mistake that breaks GCM
 * completely, which is why nothing here ever accepts a caller-supplied IV.
 *
 * The key lives in the environment, never in the repo. This module refuses to
 * run without it rather than falling back to a default, because a hardcoded
 * fallback key is indistinguishable from no encryption at all.
 */

steps.title: Bind each secret to its row
steps.note: The additional authenticated data ties a secret to its user and account. Without it, someone with write access could move another user's encrypted key into their own row and it would decrypt fine.

steps.title: Fail loudly
steps.note: A failed decryption is deliberately not caught. Turning it into an empty string would let an empty "secret" flow on into a signed request.

steps.title: Keep secrets out of logs
steps.note: Exchange error messages echo the request, so a key can hide inside an innocent-looking string. Embedded "apiKey=…" pairs are scrubbed, and long high-entropy values are redacted, while error codes like ip_not_whitelisted_for_api_key stay readable.

tours.title: Matching that never strands anyone
tours.summary: Friends Talk pairs strangers for a voice chat. The hard part isn't finding the best match; it's never leaving someone staring at a spinner.

steps.title: Preferences relax over time
steps.note: On a small server, a strict filter matches nobody, which looks exactly like a broken app. After 12 seconds the gender preference is dropped, after 25 the country filter, and the user is told. Blocks and mode are rules, so they never relax.
steps.code:
/**
 * Filters loosen the longer someone waits.
 *
 * A filter that matches nobody is indistinguishable, from the user's side,
 * from a broken app: you press call and stare at a spinner forever. On a small
 * server that is the normal case, not the edge case. So after a few seconds we
 * quietly drop the preferences the user is least likely to care about, in
 * order, and tell them we did it.
 *
 * Blocks and mode are never relaxed — those are rules, not preferences.
 */
const RELAXATION = [
  { after: 0,     ignoreGender: false, ignoreCountry: false, label: null },
  { after: 12000, ignoreGender: true,  ignoreCountry: false, label: 'gender preference' },
  { after: 25000, ignoreGender: true,  ignoreCountry: true,  label: 'country filter' }
];

steps.title: Forbidden is not the same as unlikely
steps.note: null means "never pair these two"; a negative score just means "not ideal". An earlier version treated any negative score as forbidden, so two people who had just talked could never be rematched, even when they were the only two online.

steps.title: A sweep for people whose filters relaxed
steps.note: Matching normally runs when someone joins. Two people whose filters relax past each other would otherwise wait forever with nobody to trigger a retry, so the server sweeps the queue on a timer.

tours.title: Asking four providers at once
tours.summary: RideCompare gets fares from four ride-hailing providers per search. This is the endpoint that asks them in parallel, survives the ones that fail, and caches the answer.

steps.title: A cache key that tolerates GPS jitter
steps.note: Coordinates are rounded to 4 decimal places, about 11 metres, so two searches from the same spot share a cached answer even when the phone reports slightly different positions.

steps.title: Fan out, and survive failures
steps.note: All providers are asked at once with asyncio.gather, so a search takes as long as the slowest provider, not the sum. return_exceptions=True means one provider being down removes its fares instead of failing the whole search. What I would change: failures are skipped silently, and they should be logged and shown as "unavailable".
steps.code:
providers = get_all_providers()
    tasks = [p.get_estimates(route) for p in providers]

    results_nested = await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)

    all_estimates: List[RideEstimate] = []
    for r in results_nested:
        if isinstance(r, Exception):
            continue
        all_estimates.extend(r)

steps.title: Cache the combined answer
steps.note: The whole comparison is cached in Redis with a short expiry, because fares change quickly but a user often searches the same trip twice. A cache hit still records the search, so history stays complete.
